document_title: CBD COP 9 Decision IX/16 C — Ocean Fertilization
notes: CBD COP 9 Decision IX/16 C is the Convention on Biological Diversity's first explicit international policy response to ocean fertilization as a climate-related intervention. It urges Parties and other governments, consistent with the precautionary approach, to ensure that ocean-fertilization activities do not take place until there is an adequate scientific basis for judging the risks and an effective global, transparent and science-based control and regulatory mechanism is in place. The decision allows only small-scale scientific research studies within coastal waters, subject to rigorous prior assessment and only where justified by the need to gather specific scientific data. It also states that such research should not be used for generating or selling carbon offsets or for any other commercial purpose. In the Röschel and Neumann governance review, this decision is part of the direct policy response that complements the London Convention/London Protocol regime. It is a non-binding COP decision: it does not itself issue a project permit, establish a carbon-credit methodology, quantify net CO2 removal, or authorize commercial ocean-fertilization deployment.
source: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
status_note: Adopted by CBD COP 9 in 2008; non-binding international COP decision that remains an important precautionary governance reference for ocean fertilization.

document_title: CBD COP 13 Decision XIII/14 — Climate-related Geoengineering
notes: CBD COP 13 Decision XIII/14 continues the Convention on Biological Diversity's precautionary governance of climate-related geoengineering and explicitly links CBD work to the London Protocol's 2013 marine-geoengineering amendment. It recalls earlier CBD decisions, takes note of developments under the London Convention and London Protocol, and invites Parties to the London Protocol to ratify the 2013 amendment while inviting other governments to take measures consistent with it, as appropriate. The decision also keeps biodiversity, environmental risk, transboundary implications and governance gaps in view when climate-related geoengineering is discussed. In the Röschel and Neumann review, it demonstrates institutional interaction between a biodiversity convention and the dumping/marine-geoengineering regime. It is a non-binding COP decision and does not itself bring the London Protocol amendment into force, issue an ocean-fertilization permit, approve commercial marine CDR, quantify removals, or create a carbon-credit methodology.
source: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
status_note: Adopted by CBD COP 13 in 2016; non-binding decision supporting precautionary coordination with the London Convention/London Protocol marine-geoengineering regime.

document_title: Resolution LC-LP.1(2008) on the Regulation of Ocean Fertilization
notes: Resolution LC-LP.1(2008) is the first joint London Convention/London Protocol resolution specifically addressing ocean fertilization. The Parties agreed that the scope of the two dumping instruments includes ocean-fertilization activities and concluded that ocean fertilization other than legitimate scientific research should be considered contrary to the aims of the Convention and Protocol and should not currently qualify for an exemption from the definition of dumping. The resolution therefore established a strong precautionary presumption against non-research ocean fertilization while leaving a narrowly framed research pathway to be developed through further assessment rules. Röschel and Neumann identify this resolution as a central component of the direct and explicit international governance of ocean-based negative-emissions technologies. The resolution is policy guidance adopted by Parties rather than a self-executing global project permit. It does not authorize commercial deployment, does not establish removal accounting or carbon-credit issuance, and does not by itself prove the climatic effectiveness or permanence of ocean fertilization.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention/Protocol
status_note: Adopted jointly by London Convention and London Protocol Parties in 2008; non-binding resolution that remains a core precautionary policy reference for ocean fertilization.

document_title: Resolution LC-LP.2(2010) — Assessment Framework for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization
notes: Resolution LC-LP.2(2010) adopted the Assessment Framework for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization. The framework operationalizes the research exception recognized in the 2008 resolution by providing a structured, case-by-case process for deciding whether a proposal qualifies as legitimate scientific research. It requires a scientific rationale, characterization of the proposed activity, environmental assessment, risk management, monitoring, consideration of potential impacts and uncertainties, and follow-up before an activity should proceed. The framework is designed to distinguish genuine scientific research from activities that are effectively commercial or insufficiently justified and to reduce environmental harm while knowledge remains incomplete. Röschel and Neumann highlight this assessment framework as the most developed procedural instrument in the direct governance of ocean-based negative-emissions research. It is an assessment and safeguard framework, not evidence that ocean fertilization is effective at durable net CO2 removal, not a carbon-credit methodology, and not a blanket authorization for field deployment.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention/Protocol
status_note: Adopted by London Convention/London Protocol Parties in 2010 as the assessment framework for legitimate scientific ocean-fertilization research.

document_title: Resolution LP.4(8) — Amendment to Regulate Ocean Fertilization and Other Marine Geoengineering
notes: Resolution LP.4(8), adopted in 2013, amends the London Protocol to create a treaty-based control system for marine geoengineering. It adds Article 6bis, establishes a positive-list approach under which marine-geoengineering activities covered by a new annex may not be permitted unless they are listed, and provides an environmental assessment and permitting framework in Annex 5. Ocean fertilization is the first activity listed for regulation, with legitimate scientific research capable of being considered under the assessment framework while other listed activities would require future amendment decisions. The architecture is designed to be expandable to additional marine-geoengineering techniques. Röschel and Neumann treat the amendment as the key prospective international legal structure for governing marine CDR that involves placement of matter in the ocean. The amendment has been adopted but has not entered into force, so its treaty amendments are not yet operative internationally. It does not authorize commercial ocean fertilization, establish carbon-crediting rules, or validate the effectiveness, permanence or net climate benefit of any marine CDR pathway.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Protocol
status_note: Adopted in 2013; the marine-geoengineering amendment has not entered into force internationally.

document_title: EPA Geoengineering and Marine CDR Regulatory Framework
notes: EPA's current marine geoengineering and marine carbon dioxide removal guidance explains that placing material into ocean waters can trigger federal controls under the Marine Protection, Research, and Sanctuaries Act (MPRSA), while discharges through outfalls or other point sources may instead require Clean Water Act National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System authorization. EPA states that the MPRSA implements U.S. obligations under the London Convention and emphasizes that scientific research involving ocean placement must use a suitable site and robust experimental methods designed to minimize environmental effects. The agency also states that it has serious concerns about proposed marine CDR and solar-radiation-modification activities where environmental performance is unproven, and that no marine geoengineering project has yet met the high threshold necessary to obtain an MPRSA permit. This framework is therefore regulatory and precautionary rather than a blanket authorization for ocean alkalinity enhancement, ocean fertilization, biomass sinking or other interventions. Any individual project remains subject to the applicable statutory pathway, site-specific review, environmental safeguards, public-process requirements and other federal or state approvals. The guidance does not create a carbon-crediting methodology, establish removal factors, certify permanence, or determine whether any specific marine CDR approach is environmentally acceptable.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
status_note: Current EPA regulatory guidance; source page last updated 27 March 2026.

document_title: Blue Carbon Activities in Japan
notes: Japan's national blue-carbon policy activity spans conservation and restoration of seagrass and seaweed beds, tidal flats, salt marshes and mangroves, together with measurement, research, port-area ecosystem projects and links to climate policy. The Ministry of the Environment's cross-government summary places these activities within a broader effort involving the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, the Fisheries Agency and related programmes. Policy measures include improving scientific estimation of carbon uptake and storage, supporting creation and restoration of blue-carbon ecosystems, strengthening cooperation among public agencies, researchers and industry, and developing mechanisms that can recognize climate and biodiversity benefits. These activities provide the national policy context for Japan's more specific J-Blue credit work and for the blue-carbon provisions in the Green Growth Strategy. This record describes the cross-ministry activity portfolio rather than one individual credit issuance. It does not mean that every seaweed bed, tidal flat or mangrove site automatically generates a tradable credit, and it does not authorize engineered ocean CDR. Because the identified pathways are photosynthesis- and biomass-based coastal or macroalgal systems, the direct carbon-pump mechanism is BCP; MCP is not assigned without evidence of explicit microbial/RDOC processes.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Japan

document_title: J-Blue Credit Pilot and Certificate Issuance
notes: The J-Blue Credit pilot developed a Japanese project-level mechanism for certifying and transacting carbon associated with coastal and marine ecosystem activities, particularly conservation, creation and restoration of seagrass and seaweed beds and related coastal habitats. The programme emerged from national blue-carbon research and port-policy work and provides a practical bridge between quantified coastal carbon benefits, third-party review/certification and voluntary purchasing. The early pilot and certificate issuances demonstrated how projects could document boundaries, activities, monitoring evidence and estimated CO2 absorption for recognition as J-Blue Credits. The mechanism is voluntary and project-specific; it does not create compliance obligations under a national emissions trading system and it does not mean that all protected coastal carbon is additional removal. Credit quantities depend on the approved methodology, baseline, monitoring and certification rules applying to each project. This record is kept separate from Japan's broader Green Growth Strategy and cross-ministry blue-carbon activities because it represents an operational crediting/certification instrument. The relevant ecosystem pathways use biological production and burial, so BCP is the appropriate direct carbon-pump tag; MCP is not inferred.
source: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT)
status_note: Operational Japanese voluntary blue-carbon crediting and certification initiative; early pilot certificates were issued by 2022 and the mechanism has continued to evolve.

document_title: Guidance for Evaluating Conservation and Restoration of Seagrass Beds and Tidal Flats Using Blue Carbon
notes: Japan's Ministry of the Environment issued this guidance to evaluate conservation, restoration and creation of seaweed beds and tidal flats while explicitly incorporating blue-carbon and other ecosystem functions into project evaluation. The guidance is intended to make project outcomes more comparable and evidence-based by linking ecological condition, restoration performance and climate-related functions to survey and evaluation practice. It is particularly relevant to seagrass beds and intertidal habitats because these systems can protect existing organic-carbon stores and, when successfully restored, create additional biological uptake and sediment accumulation. The document should nevertheless be distinguished from Japan's voluntary blue-carbon crediting arrangements: it is an environmental evaluation and restoration guidance instrument, not a credit-issuance rule, a national greenhouse-gas inventory methodology, or an automatic demonstration of additionality and permanence for a tradable carbon unit. Carbon benefits therefore depend on site-specific ecological recovery, baseline conditions, monitoring design and the durability of restored habitat. The guidance complements Japan's broader Satoumi, seaweed-bed and tidal-flat policies by providing an evaluation-oriented bridge between habitat management and blue-carbon evidence, and it can support future policy learning without predetermining market eligibility.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Japan
status_note: Published by Japan's Ministry of the Environment in 2025 and retained as current guidance.

document_title: Action Plan for Carbon Dioxide Peaking Before 2030
notes: China's State Council Action Plan for Carbon Dioxide Peaking Before 2030 is the principal national implementation plan for the pre-2030 carbon-peaking objective. Its ecosystem-sink measures explicitly include integrated protection and restoration of marine ecosystems, enhancement of the carbon-sequestration capacity of mangroves, seagrass beds and salt marshes, and development of marine-carbon-sink investigation, assessment, monitoring and accounting capacity. These provisions connect coastal blue-carbon restoration with the national carbon-peaking policy system and provide a high-level mandate for later marine monitoring standards, restoration programmes and provincial implementation plans. The plan is enabling and coordinative rather than an operating marine offset rule. It does not establish marine-carbon eligibility in the national CCER market, create a credit registry, prescribe project-level additionality or permanence requirements, or authorize engineered marine CDR. The engineering pathways are limited to the specific ecosystems named in the policy. Accordingly, the record uses BCP as the direct carbon-pump mechanism and does not assign MCP simply because coastal ecosystems contain microbial processes. The plan remains active toward its 2030 implementation horizon.
source: State Council of the People's Republic of China
status_note: Adopted national action plan implementing China's pre-2030 carbon-peaking objective; marine ecosystem restoration and carbon-sink monitoring provisions remain relevant through the 2030 horizon.

document_title: MEE Response to CPPCC Proposal No. 04932 on Establishing a Marine Carbon Sink and Negative Emissions System
notes: China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment response to CPPCC Proposal No. 04932 provides an unusually explicit statement of the central-government position on marine carbon sinks, monitoring and carbon-market treatment. The response describes protection, restoration and monitoring work for mangroves, seagrass beds and coastal salt marshes and notes carbon-stock and flux monitoring in nine coastal cities. It emphasizes that carbon sinks eligible for market treatment must be generated by anthropogenic activities, be additional to business-as-usual outcomes, be authentic and be uniquely accounted for. It also states that China's national voluntary greenhouse-gas reduction market is intended to operate under unified rules and that marine carbon-sink activities can be developed as project types within that national voluntary-market framework when eligible methodologies and requirements are met. On that basis, the Ministry does not support creating separate local marine negative-emissions trading pilots merely to establish an alternative market architecture. The response calls for stronger ecosystem protection and restoration, improved monitoring and a dynamic marine-carbon data foundation, study of feasible project types and implementation pathways, and gradual expansion of market support. It is an official policy response rather than a binding regulation or approved marine methodology; it does not itself issue CCER credits or make every marine sink activity immediately tradable.
source: Ministry of Ecology and Environment, China
status_note: Official Ministry of Ecology and Environment response dated 23 July 2025 and published on the ministry website in November 2025.

document_title: Developing a National Dataset for Coastal Wetland Blue Carbon in Aotearoa New Zealand
notes: This Ministry for the Environment-commissioned technical work develops a quantitative national evidence base for coastal-wetland blue carbon in Aotearoa New Zealand. The study assembles available measurements, identifies geographic and methodological data gaps, and proposes a research pathway for improving estimates of carbon stocks and sequestration in coastal wetlands. The Ministry states that the dataset can inform restoration policy, greenhouse-gas accounting and consideration of future carbon-crediting or other recognition mechanisms, while the associated technical work emphasizes the steps needed before coastal-wetland removals could be treated with high integrity. The work is therefore enabling infrastructure rather than a crediting decision. It does not by itself add coastal wetlands to the New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme, amend the national greenhouse-gas inventory, establish project additionality, or provide a universal default factor for every estuary or habitat. Follow-on research is expected to strengthen spatial coverage, comparability and uncertainty treatment. The record is classified primarily as research and MRV preparation because its most important policy contribution is to reduce information barriers for future decisions on restoration, inventory reporting and potential market recognition.
source: Ministry for the Environment / The Nature Conservancy New Zealand
status_note: Technical report published 10 December 2025; the Ministry describes follow-on work to improve the national evidence base.

document_title: New Zealand's Second Emissions Reduction Plan 2026–30 — Amended January 2026
notes: New Zealand's amended second emissions reduction plan covers the 2026–2030 emissions-budget period and makes recognition of non-forest carbon removals a national policy workstream. The current sector-policy text explicitly identifies coastal vegetation management, including wetlands, mangroves and seagrasses, as a blue-carbon option that can protect existing sinks and establish new ones. It also lists marine ecosystems and ocean fertilisation among examples of removal activities while stressing that many biological systems can act as either sinks or sources when vegetation is removed or ecosystems are disturbed. The technical annex describes a staged approach: develop an assessment framework, build methodologies that are appropriate for New Zealand and internationally aligned, expand accounting for non-forest land uses, and consider mechanisms that could recognise additional removals, with the New Zealand Emissions Trading Scheme identified as one possible mechanism. The plan does not automatically make blue-carbon or ocean-fertilisation activities eligible for the NZ ETS, does not approve field intervention, and does not replace environmental or international-law requirements. It provides the policy basis for evidence assessment and possible future recognition. The January 2026 amendment primarily reflects revised agricultural-emissions policy while retaining the wider non-forest-removals framework.
source: Ministry for the Environment, New Zealand
status_note: Amended plan published 29 January 2026 and effective for the 2026–2030 emissions-budget period.

document_title: Real Decreto 191/2026, de 11 de marzo, para la conservación de las praderas de angiospermas marinas en el Mediterráneo español
notes: Spain's Royal Decree 191/2026 creates a binding national framework for conserving Mediterranean marine-angiosperm meadows, principally Posidonia oceanica and Cymodocea nodosa. The decree requires mapping and knowledge improvement, establishes protective rules for activities that can damage the meadows, regulates anchoring and encourages lower-impact mooring arrangements, and provides for monitoring, research, restoration and enforcement. Its climate relevance arises from safeguarding seagrass ecosystems that store substantial carbon in biomass and sediments, but the decree is fundamentally a habitat-protection regulation rather than a carbon-crediting rule. It does not assign tradable removal units, prescribe project additionality, establish a national blue-carbon registry or guarantee that restoration will yield a quantified net removal. The legal text also operates alongside wider environmental-impact and marine-management requirements, and potential activities affecting these habitats remain subject to applicable assessment and authorization procedures. This record therefore treats the decree as a binding protective and restoration-enabling instrument with direct relevance to seagrass carbon stores, while avoiding conversion of the conservation obligation into an unsupported carbon-market claim. It supersedes the earlier short database description and uses the official BOE legal text as the controlling source.
source: Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge, Spain

document_title: Scottish Blue Carbon Action Plan — Saltmarsh Actions
notes: Scotland's Blue Carbon Action Plan treats saltmarsh as one of four priority blue-carbon habitat groups and pairs restoration policy with a substantial evidence programme. The plan notes that saltmarsh is among the habitats for which international greenhouse-gas inventory guidance is comparatively mature, but further Scottish data are needed on carbon stocks, sequestration and greenhouse-gas exchange. Actions include multi-year flux-tower measurements intended to quantify net greenhouse-gas balance, support through the UK Blue Carbon Evidence Partnership to improve the evidence needed for inventory treatment, and NatureScot work to map restoration opportunities and help prioritize investment. The plan also links protection and restoration decisions to the principle that conserving existing carbon stores is generally lower risk than attempting to recreate them after degradation. These actions do not constitute a Scottish carbon-credit protocol and do not guarantee that every restoration site is a net sink; methane, nitrous oxide, erosion, hydrology and baseline condition can materially affect net climate benefit. The record therefore captures the policy as a combined restoration, monitoring and inventory-readiness programme. Where future finance or markets are considered, the action plan still requires robust evidence and appropriate accounting before climate claims can be treated as verified removals.
source: Scottish Government — Marine Directorate
status_note: Published September 2025; actions scheduled through 2028/29

document_title: Scottish Blue Carbon Action Plan — Seagrass Actions
notes: The Scottish Blue Carbon Action Plan identifies seagrass as a high-priority habitat for protection, restoration and evidence development because intact meadows can store carbon in vegetation and sediments while also supporting biodiversity, water quality and coastal resilience. The plan calls for better baseline information, standardized survey and monitoring practice, and improved estimates of carbon stocks and sequestration so that projects can be assessed consistently. It highlights work to develop and trial guidance and protocols on practical restoration projects, including activity supported through the Scottish Marine Environmental Enhancement Fund and more than £2 million of SSEN Distribution support over four years. The policy also calls for assessment of how existing or potential protection measures affect seagrass condition and carbon stores. Scotland does not treat these actions as automatic carbon-credit issuance: restoration success, additionality, permanence, disturbance risk and site-specific sediment dynamics remain important uncertainties. The record is therefore classified as restoration plus MRV and methodology preparation. The action plan's broader evidence framework also notes that seagrass is one of the coastal habitats for which IPCC guidance offers a clearer route toward greenhouse-gas inventory treatment than several emerging blue-carbon stores, but national implementation still depends on appropriate data and accounting decisions.
source: Scottish Government — Marine Directorate
status_note: Published September 2025; actions scheduled through 2028/29

document_title: Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global ONCE) — UN Ocean Decade Programme
notes: Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global-ONCE) is an endorsed UN Decade of Ocean Science programme led by Xiamen University, with an official programme period from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2030. The Ocean Decade description states that the programme will undertake and facilitate the science needed to evaluate and implement eco-technological interventions that could enhance ocean carbon sequestration, including restoration of impacted marine ecosystems, land-sea integrated management, manipulation of upwelling, microbial-driven carbon sequestration, and adjustment of nutrients, dissolved oxygen and pH. Its institutional functions are broader than a single technology project: it is intended to build an international network of field stations and research facilities, co-design interdisciplinary research, develop an evaluation framework for mitigation and adaptation approaches, coordinate capacity building, and improve equitable policy, governance and societal understanding. A 2025 peer-reviewed declaration by early-career ocean professionals describes Global-ONCE as a platform spanning 79 research groups in 33 countries and more than 1,500 participants and calls for stronger basic and applied mCDR research, blue-carbon protection and restoration, international cooperation, monitoring, capacity building and attention to precaution and equity. These descriptions support classification as a research, coordination and evidence-building programme. They do not constitute blanket legal authorization for ocean CDR deployment, do not certify a carbon-credit methodology, and do not establish a quantified programme-wide carbon-removal obligation or guarantee that any intervention will be environmentally acceptable or commercially deployable.
source: UNESCO-IOC Ocean Decade
status_note: Active UN Ocean Decade Programme with an official 1 January 2022–31 December 2030 programme period; it coordinates research, evaluation, capacity building and governance work rather than granting deployment permits or issuing carbon credits.

document_title: Blue Carbon Canada
notes: Blue Carbon Canada is an Ocean Decade research partnership designed to quantify current and potential future carbon storage in Canadian salt marshes, seagrass beds, kelp forests and marine sediments, evaluate pressures such as bottom disturbance, and connect ecological evidence with policy and economic valuation. Its continuing relevance is confirmed in Fisheries and Oceans Canada's 2026–27 Departmental Plan, which identifies partnership work with Blue Carbon Canada to measure carbon in eelgrass, kelp forests and salt marshes and to assess carbon storage and economic value. The departmental plan explicitly connects this evidence to emissions accounting, marine spatial planning, marine protected areas, restoration priorities and possible conservation-finance or blue-carbon-market applications. The project therefore functions as national research infrastructure for policy decisions rather than as a carbon-credit scheme. It does not mean that all measured Canadian blue-carbon stores are included in the national greenhouse-gas inventory, that disturbance avoidance automatically generates offsets, or that kelp carbon is treated as durable removal without further evidence. The 2022–2028 project period allows repeated measurement and policy translation, and the database retains the original programme record while adding the 2026 federal planning context instead of creating a duplicate entry for the same Blue Carbon Canada research initiative.
source: UNESCO-IOC Ocean Decade / University of Victoria
status_note: Ocean Decade project active from July 2022 to August 2028; Fisheries and Oceans Canada's 2026–27 Departmental Plan confirms continuing federal partnership and policy use.

document_title: C-BLUES — Carbon Sequestration in Blue Ecosystems
notes: C-BLUES (Carbon Sequestration in BLUe EcoSystems; Grant Agreement 101137844) is a Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Action implemented from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2028 under the EU-China international-cooperation topic on blue carbon. CORDIS reports a total project cost of EUR 4,244,081.25 and an EU contribution of EUR 4,244,080.50. The project investigates carbon stocks, sequestration and greenhouse-gas fluxes across major blue ecosystems, including seagrass meadows, tidal marshes, mangroves, macroalgae and macroalgal mariculture. Its work includes spatial mapping, field and experimental measurements, harmonisation of methodological best practices and standard operating procedures, assessment of management interventions, regional and global modelling, and analysis of legal and institutional barriers to incorporating blue-ecosystem greenhouse-gas fluxes into national reporting. C-BLUES also aims to provide scientific input relevant to future refinement of greenhouse-gas inventory guidance, including possible future work connected with the IPCC Wetlands Supplement. These outputs justify tags for monitoring, carbon accounting research and policy coordination, but they must not be confused with adopted regulatory requirements: C-BLUES does not itself create a legally binding MRV system, approve an IPCC methodology, certify blue-carbon credits, establish a compliance market, or authorize restoration or aquaculture deployment. Its principal function is to build the evidence, datasets, methods and cross-regional research capacity needed for later policy and accounting decisions.
source: European Commission CORDIS / Horizon Europe
status_note: Active Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Action, 1 April 2024–31 March 2028; methodological and SOP outputs are research products and are not themselves adopted IPCC, UNFCCC or carbon-market standards.

document_title: Blue Carbon Accelerator Fund
notes: The Blue Carbon Accelerator Fund (BCAF) was an Australia-supported partnership implemented with IUCN to accelerate high-quality coastal blue-carbon projects in developing countries. It operated through readiness and implementation support, helping project proponents improve scientific baselines, restoration planning, governance, safeguards, community engagement, financing strategies and investment readiness. The programme supported a portfolio of projects focused on mangroves, seagrasses, tidal wetlands and associated coastal ecosystems and sought to mobilize finance by improving project quality and credibility. Some supported projects may pursue carbon-market or results-based finance, but BCAF itself was not a universal crediting standard and did not issue a single fungible BCAF carbon unit. Its grants and technical assistance also did not constitute deployment permits; projects remained subject to national law, tenure, environmental safeguards and any certification rules selected by individual proponents. The programme is relevant to negative-emissions engineering because it directly supported conservation and restoration capable of increasing or protecting coastal carbon stocks, while its policy role was principally funding, capacity building, project preparation, international cooperation and social/environmental safeguards.

document_title: International Partnership for Blue Carbon
notes: The International Partnership for Blue Carbon is a voluntary global partnership launched by Australia in 2015 to connect governments, intergovernmental organizations, research institutions, NGOs and practitioners working on coastal blue carbon. It promotes conservation and restoration of mangroves, seagrasses, tidal marshes and other coastal blue-carbon ecosystems through policy exchange, scientific knowledge, capacity building, project development and international coordination. The partnership helps members integrate blue carbon into climate, biodiversity, coastal-management and sustainable-development policy and provides a forum for sharing methodologies, finance approaches and implementation experience. Its governance effect is enabling rather than legally binding: membership does not create treaty obligations, authorize restoration activity, certify carbon removals or establish a common international credit registry. Carbon-market projects associated with member organizations remain subject to the relevant project standard, national policy and monitoring rules. The partnership is therefore recorded primarily as an international coordination and policy-planning mechanism with direct relevance to coastal blue-carbon restoration. Its carbon-pump tag is BCP because the targeted ecosystems rely on biological production and organic-carbon storage; no additional microbial or carbonate-pump mechanism is inferred automatically.

document_title: Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier CCT3 — Manage Coastal Saltmarsh and Its Vegetation
notes: England's Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier action CCT3 provides a five-year land-management payment for maintaining coastal saltmarsh in good condition and restoring saltmarsh in unfavourable condition. Current guidance lists an annual payment rate of £724 per hectare and describes outcomes that include expansion and improvement of priority saltmarsh habitat, greater resilience to climate change, and contribution to carbon capture and storage alongside biodiversity, flood-management and water-quality benefits. The payment is tied to eligible management requirements and is not a purchase of quantified carbon credits. It does not establish project baselines, additionality tests, permanence buffers, carbon ownership rules or verified tonnes of CO2e, and it should not be interpreted as allowing double claiming with a separate carbon market. Climate benefit depends on the condition and hydrology of the marsh, avoided loss of existing soil carbon and, where restoration succeeds, renewed sediment and organic-carbon accumulation. The record is therefore classified as ecological-compensation and restoration support rather than a crediting mechanism. The updated guidance is useful for the database because it demonstrates a concrete public-finance instrument that can support blue-carbon habitat outcomes without converting those outcomes into a formal offset commodity.
source: Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs / Rural Payments Agency, United Kingdom
status_note: Published 10 September 2025; current official guidance updated 7 May 2026.

document_title: Mikoko Pamoja Community-Based Mangrove Carbon Project
notes: Mikoko Pamoja is a community-based mangrove conservation and restoration initiative in Gazi Bay, Kenya that uses verified blue-carbon finance to support both ecosystem management and local development. The project became an early and widely cited example of a mangrove project raising revenue through the voluntary sale of carbon credits, with Plan Vivo certification providing the project-level framework for quantification, monitoring and issuance. The 2025 Ocean Panel working paper on ocean finance highlights Mikoko Pamoja as an example in which carbon revenue has supported continued mangrove planting and conservation while also providing community benefits, including improved freshwater access and support for classrooms and educational materials. The case is particularly relevant to ONCE policy because it combines a measurable coastal carbon sink with crediting, community participation and safeguards rather than treating carbon as the only project objective. The Ocean Panel discussion stresses that credible baselines, ecological and social factors, local traditions and safeguards are essential to avoid harmful outcomes or overstated climate claims. Mikoko Pamoja therefore demonstrates a functioning voluntary blue-carbon finance model, but its scope remains project-specific. It does not create a Kenyan national compliance carbon market, does not automatically validate other mangrove projects, and should not be interpreted as proof that every mangrove restoration activity produces equivalent or additional removals. Carbon accounting, permanence, leakage, community rights and site-specific ecological conditions remain material to credit integrity.
source: Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute / local community partners / United Nations Environment Programme
status_note: Active community-based mangrove carbon project with Plan Vivo certification and voluntary credit sales; it is a site-specific project mechanism rather than a Kenyan national compliance-market rule.

notes: Ramsar Resolution XIII.14 is a dedicated international policy instrument on coastal blue carbon. It calls on Contracting Parties to conserve, restore and sustainably manage coastal blue-carbon ecosystems, particularly mangroves, tidal marshes and seagrass meadows, and recognizes their climate-mitigation, adaptation, biodiversity and ecosystem-service benefits. The resolution encourages improved mapping, inventories, monitoring and assessment of blue-carbon ecosystems; use of relevant IPCC greenhouse-gas inventory guidance; integration of coastal wetlands into climate and biodiversity planning; cooperation across relevant international processes; and consideration of financing and implementation opportunities. Röschel and Neumann cite the resolution when explaining how the Ramsar system can provide indirect governance and policy support for blue-carbon interventions. The resolution is non-binding and does not establish a mandatory restoration area, a standardized project-level carbon-credit methodology, an offset registry, or a quantified guarantee of additional CO2 removal. Its principal function is to strengthen policy planning, evidence, conservation and restoration of coastal carbon-rich wetlands.

document_title: Act Amending the Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Act and the Pollution Control Act (Expanded Geographical Scope) — Act No. 54 of 19 June 2026
notes: Norway's Act No. 54 of 19 June 2026 amends the Pollution Control Act and the Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Act to extend legal authority over activities with important offshore carbon-management and marine-geoengineering implications. The amendments provide a clearer basis for regulating dumping, placement of material and marine geoengineering beyond Norwegian territorial waters and the exclusive economic zone where Norway acts consistently with applicable international obligations. They also support implementation of European emissions-trading rules relevant to transport of greenhouse gases for geological storage. This is a framework law: it expands statutory competence and regulatory reach but does not itself approve ocean fertilisation, alkalinity enhancement, offshore injection, a CO2 transport network or any particular storage site. Project-level operations remain subject to applicable sectoral regulations, storage licences, pollution-control requirements, monitoring and environmental safeguards. The law is particularly important for the database because it links marine environmental jurisdiction with the rapidly developing cross-border CO2 transport and storage sector, while preserving a precautionary permitting structure. It should not be read as a carbon-credit methodology or as evidence that a specific marine intervention has satisfied environmental-integrity, permanence or monitoring requirements.

notes: This National Academies consensus study, publicly released on 8 December 2021, evaluates six broad ocean-based carbon dioxide removal approaches: nutrient fertilization; artificial upwelling and downwelling; seaweed cultivation; marine and coastal ecosystem recovery; ocean alkalinity enhancement; and electrochemical processes. notes: The Manual for the Creation of Blue Carbon Projects in Europe and the Mediterranean provides practical project-development guidance for coastal blue-carbon conservation and restoration. References to carbon finance or certification are options for project developers rather than automatic credit issuance. Quantified climate benefits still require project-specific baselines, additionality, monitoring, verification, permanence and leakage treatment under whichever standard or public programme is used.

document_title: Mangrove Breakthrough Financial Roadmap
notes: The Mangrove Breakthrough Financial Roadmap provides a voluntary international financing pathway for scaling mangrove conservation, protection and restoration toward the Mangrove Breakthrough's 2030 objectives. It examines how public budgets, philanthropy, concessional capital and private investment can be combined through blended-finance structures and investable business models, including blue-carbon finance, sustainable aquaculture, fisheries, tourism and other activities linked to healthy mangrove ecosystems. The 2025 Ocean Panel ocean-finance working paper cites the Mangrove Breakthrough as a key blue-carbon finance initiative and describes an ambition to unlock approximately USD 4 billion for mangrove action. Current Mangrove Breakthrough communications likewise frame the USD 4 billion figure as a public-private-philanthropic finance mobilization goal associated with halting mangrove loss, restoring degraded mangroves and expanding effective protection by 2030. The figure should therefore be interpreted as a mobilization target or investment need, not as evidence that a separate USD 4 billion fund has already been fully capitalized or legally appropriated. The roadmap can help shape carbon-credit investment and other financing structures, but it does not itself issue credits, establish a registry, impose a mandatory MRV methodology, approve projects or guarantee investment returns. Project-level additionality, permanence, carbon accounting, biodiversity safeguards, community rights and legal authorization remain dependent on the standards and jurisdictions under which individual activities are implemented.
source: Global Mangrove Alliance, UN Climate Change High-Level Champions and Systemiq
status_note: Published in 2023 and used as an active voluntary finance roadmap for the Mangrove Breakthrough; the widely cited USD 4 billion figure is a finance-mobilization ambition, not proof of fully committed or disbursed fund capital.

document_title: Blue Carbon Ecosystems NDC Implementation and Investment Plan 2025–2035 — Final Plan
notes: The Government of Kenya officially launched the final Blue Carbon Ecosystems NDC Implementation and Investment Plan 2025–2035 at the eleventh Our Ocean Conference. The plan consolidates blue-carbon obligations across the 2020–2030 and 2031–2035 NDC cycles into an actionable national investment framework for mangroves, seagrasses and coastal wetlands. It includes restoration and conservation targets, a national MRV architecture, high-integrity carbon accounting aligned with Paris Agreement Article 6, benefit-sharing and institutional coordination measures, and a financing architecture intended to mobilize approximately USD 620 million by 2035. The plan is an implementation and investment framework rather than a project permit; individual restoration, market and infrastructure activities remain subject to applicable approvals and safeguards.
source: Government of Kenya — Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Forestry; Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs

document_title: Carbon Dioxide Removal Leadership Act of 2026 (H.R. 9975)
notes: The House bill would require the U.S. Department of Energy to procure net carbon dioxide removal from ambient air or seawater against rising annual targets and would require lifecycle accounting, independent third-party verification and federal standards for measurement, monitoring, reporting and verification. The ONCE-relevant component is direct removal from seawater; the bill also covers non-marine direct-air approaches. It was introduced but not enacted, so the procurement obligations, tonnage targets and MRV rules are proposals rather than active requirements.
source: United States Congress / U.S. Government Publishing Office
status_note: Introduced in the House of Representatives on 27 July 2026 and referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce; not enacted.

subnational_area: Fitzroy Basin, Peel-Harvey and South West catchments, and Ord River floodplain
document_title: NESP Project 1.15 — Coastal Wetland Restoration for Carbon Accounting
notes: This completed National Environmental Science Program project examined whether historically modified coastal wetlands could be restored and financed through blue-carbon markets. It developed a site-selection process, estimated carbon-abatement potential, assessed regulatory and policy constraints, compared carbon-price scenarios, and evaluated ecological, cultural and economic co-benefits. The project identified potentially eligible restoration areas in the Fitzroy Basin and Peel-Harvey case-study regions and reported modelled annual abatement estimates for those areas. It also found that the assessed Ord River sites did not satisfy the relevant restoration eligibility conditions. The work provides feasibility, accounting and investment evidence, but it did not itself rewet the identified sites, issue carbon credits, create an approved national methodology, or grant a deployment authorization.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Completed NESP Marine and Coastal Hub project with published findings, datasets and restoration-site assessment outputs.

document_title: NESP Project 4.12 — Gulf of Carpentaria Mangrove Dieback: Research to Support Recovery Management
notes: This National Environmental Science Program project evaluates the condition and recovery of shoreline mangroves damaged by major dieback events in the Gulf of Carpentaria. It updates condition maps, conducts aerial and field monitoring, quantifies carbon in damaged, undamaged and recovering stands, evaluates protection and restoration options, and includes mitigation works or small-scale trials where feasible. The project is designed to support a costed management response plan and future rehabilitation decisions. Its carbon component measures changes in mangrove carbon stocks and supports restoration planning, but the project does not establish a carbon-credit methodology, authorize commercial deployment, set a quantified removal target, or report issued credits or independently verified additional removals.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub
status_note: Active NESP project; monitoring and recovery research continued through at least 2026.

document_title: ARC Linkage Project LP250200320 — Advancing Seagrass Restoration to Ecologically Relevant Scales in Australia
notes: This Australian Research Council Linkage Project develops the evidence and practical framework needed to expand seagrass restoration to ecologically relevant scales. It evaluates propagule supply, best-practice site selection, recovery of ecosystem services and the design of large-scale restoration trials. The official grant record explicitly identifies carbon storage and capture as benefits of restored seagrass and links the work to national climate and biodiversity targets. The project runs from 2026 to 2029 and includes university, government, foundation and Traditional Owner partners. It is a research and demonstration programme, not a binding restoration mandate, carbon-credit method, project permit, quantified national removal target or evidence of verified credits.
source: Australian Research Council

document_title: MAR-CO2 — Measurement and Reporting for Responsible Marine CO2 Removal
notes: MAR-CO2 is a Horizon Europe project developing fit-for-purpose monitoring, reporting and verification systems for marine carbon-dioxide removal. It will co-design, refine and test tools for quantifying removal additionality and durability, assessing ecological risks and co-benefits, and developing governance arrangements that support transparency, fairness and public trust. The project combines observations, experiments, modelling, ecology, social science, governance and digital-twin methods, and tests the tools under operational mCDR conditions with industry partners. The grant was signed in May 2026 and the project runs from August 2026 to July 2030. It is an international research and standard-development programme; it does not itself issue carbon credits, create binding EU permitting rules, approve commercial deployments or guarantee that tested removals will qualify under a compliance market.
source: European Commission — Horizon Europe / CORDIS
status_note: Horizon Europe project active from 1 August 2026 to 31 July 2030; grant agreement signed on 6 May 2026.

document_title: Bringing Wetlands to Market Phase 1: Nitrogen and Coastal Blue Carbon
notes: This NOAA-supported collaborative research project examined how salt-marsh carbon storage and greenhouse-gas fluxes respond to nitrogen pollution, tidal conditions and wetland management. It developed monitoring, modeling and practitioner-facing tools intended to make coastal blue-carbon information usable in conservation and restoration decisions. Outputs included a coastal-wetland greenhouse-gas model, guidance on applying the Verified Carbon Standard methodology for tidal-wetland and seagrass restoration, economic and policy communication materials, and stakeholder training. The project helped establish the scientific and procedural foundation for considering wetland carbon finance. It was a completed research and capacity-building project; it did not itself authorize restoration work, create a compliance market, register a carbon project or issue carbon credits.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from November 2011 to June 2015.

document_title: Bringing Wetlands to Market Phase 2: Expanding Blue Carbon Implementation
notes: The second phase expanded the earlier Massachusetts blue-carbon work into a broader implementation-oriented research programme for New England and the Mid-Atlantic coast. The project verified and generalized a model for estimating wetland greenhouse-gas fluxes and potential carbon storage from a limited set of accessible environmental variables. It also completed a carbon-market feasibility assessment for the proposed Herring River wetland restoration project and produced tools, education products and guidance for managers and decision-makers. The programme reduced information and transaction barriers associated with blue-carbon project preparation, but it remained a scientific assessment and capacity-building activity. It did not approve the Herring River project, establish a mandatory accounting rule, register offsets or demonstrate that any credits had been issued.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from January 2016 to September 2019.

document_title: Pacific Northwest Carbon Stocks and Blue Carbon Database Project
notes: This regional collaborative project conducted the first comprehensive assessment of carbon stocks across major Pacific Northwest tidal-wetland classes and created a user-oriented regional blue-carbon database. Field and compiled data covered seagrass, low marsh, high marsh and forested tidal wetlands across distinct coastal settings. The work was designed to support greenhouse-gas accounting, restoration planning, conservation prioritization and assessment of possible carbon-finance opportunities. It strengthened the evidence base needed by managers and project developers rather than establishing a market mechanism itself. The completed project did not authorize a restoration intervention, certify a methodology, register a carbon-credit project or guarantee that mapped carbon stocks represented additional and creditable removals. Subsequent project-level feasibility and policy decisions remained separate steps.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from November 2016 to December 2019.

document_title: Feasibility Planning for Pacific Northwest Blue Carbon Finance Projects
notes: This catalyst project assessed whether carbon finance could contribute to tidal-wetland conservation and restoration in the Pacific Northwest. The project evaluated baseline and restoration scenarios and examined financial feasibility for candidate sites in the Snohomish, Skagit and Coos estuaries. It drew on regional carbon-stock data and the Verified Carbon Standard tidal-wetland and seagrass methodology to identify opportunities, data gaps, transaction constraints and next steps for project development. The work supplied project proponents, resource managers and potential investors with a structured feasibility assessment. It did not constitute validation or registration under a carbon standard, did not authorize work at any candidate site and did not demonstrate that credits were issued. Project-level additionality, ownership, permanence, leakage and monitoring requirements would still require formal assessment.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed catalyst project, implemented from September 2018 to December 2019.

subnational_area: Texas and the Gulf of Mexico coast
document_title: Bringing Wetlands to Market on the Gulf Coast
notes: This NOAA-funded science-transfer project adapted lessons from the Massachusetts Bringing Wetlands to Market initiative for Gulf Coast audiences. It used outreach dialogues, stakeholder needs assessment and communication products to explain coastal blue carbon, natural capital and the potential role of carbon finance in supporting wetland restoration and conservation. The work connected landowners, resource managers, researchers and government participants and documented regional questions, constraints and priorities for future blue-carbon research and demonstration projects. It primarily transferred knowledge and strengthened networks; it did not generate a new regional carbon-stock inventory, approve a restoration project, establish a crediting methodology or issue carbon credits. Recommendations and finance opportunities identified through the project remained non-binding and required subsequent project development and verification.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed science-transfer project, implemented from June 2016 to October 2018.

document_title: Land Use and Environmental Effects on Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Carbon Sequestration in Pacific Northwest Tidal Wetlands
notes: This collaborative research project quantified how greenhouse-gas emissions, carbon accumulation and net climate benefits vary among Pacific Northwest tidal-wetland types and land uses. Field work across multiple estuaries examined marshes, swamps, restored wetlands and altered lands, while the project expanded the regional blue-carbon database and contributed data for validation of a national methane-emissions model. Results supported development of regional calculators, mapping tools and climate-mitigation policy applications. The project strengthened accounting evidence by showing that methane emissions and carbon accumulation depend on salinity, hydrology, restoration history and local site conditions. It did not create a regulatory inventory requirement, certify credits or authorize restoration. Use of the results in carbon accounting or markets still requires project-specific baselines, uncertainty treatment and verification.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from October 2020 to September 2024.

document_title: Testing Low-cost, Ultra-portable, Carbon Dioxide Sensors for Monitoring Salt Marsh Ecosystem Services, Resilience, and Restoration
notes: This multi-reserve catalyst project tested low-cost, portable sensor packages for measuring carbon-dioxide fluxes, temperature and humidity in salt-marsh environments. The project responded to the high cost and labor requirements of conventional greenhouse-gas monitoring and worked with reserve staff to improve instrument usability under routine field conditions. It produced shared field experience, datasets and a monitoring protocol intended to expand in-situ carbon-flux measurement capacity across the National Estuarine Research Reserve System. The programme supported MRV-related research and restoration evaluation but did not create a legally required monitoring standard, certify the sensor system for carbon-credit verification or establish that its measurements alone are sufficient for offset issuance. Longer time series, calibration, quality assurance and project-specific accounting remain necessary.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed catalyst project, implemented from October 2023 to September 2024.

document_title: A Long-Term Perspective on Tidal Wetland Restoration: Vegetation Development, Elevation Capital, and Carbon Sequestration in the Oldest Projects Along the U.S. West Coast
notes: This multi-site project assessed some of the oldest tidal-marsh restoration sites on the United States West Coast and compared them with reference marshes. The work examined vegetation development, elevation capital, carbon storage and long-term recovery across sites in California, Oregon and Washington. Outputs included regional datasets, scientific publications and management guidance intended to improve future restoration design and monitoring. By studying projects several decades after intervention, the programme addressed evidence gaps that cannot be resolved through short project cycles. It was a completed research assessment and did not itself implement new restoration, approve project permits, establish a carbon-credit baseline or issue credits. Transfer of the findings to other wetland types or regions requires consideration of local sediment supply, hydrology, vegetation and sea-level conditions.
source: NERRS Science Collaborative / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status_note: Completed collaborative research project, implemented from October 2022 to September 2024.

document_title: Assessing Blue Carbon Storage at Restoration Sites of Various Ages and Morphologies
notes: This ongoing NOAA project quantifies carbon stocks, greenhouse-gas fluxes, sediment carbon and biomass at coastal sites restored through different techniques and at different times. Study designs include thin-layer placement of dredged sediment, living shorelines and beneficial use of dredged material to construct estuarine islands. The objective is to determine how quickly restored habitats develop carbon-storage functions comparable with natural systems and how restoration design affects possible eligibility for carbon offsets. The work directly supports blue-carbon accounting and restoration evaluation but remains a research programme. It does not certify any site, establish ownership of carbon benefits, approve offset issuance or replace the additionality, permanence, leakage and verification requirements of an applicable carbon standard.
source: National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science (NCCOS), NOAA
status_note: Ongoing NCCOS research project that began in September 2022.

document_title: Ecological Impacts of Sea Level Rise on Flood Protection and Blue Carbon Capture in Pacific Northwest Wetlands
notes: This NCCOS research project evaluated how restored and natural tidal marshes and forested coastal wetlands in Coos Bay, Oregon, and Grays Bay, Washington, may provide flood buffering and blue-carbon benefits under sea-level-rise scenarios. The project combined hydrodynamic modeling, wetland-elevation modeling, existing datasets and new field observations of greenhouse-gas emissions and carbon sequestration. document_title: Isometric Direct Ocean Capture and Storage Protocol, Version 1.1
notes: This Isometric protocol specifies requirements for calculating net atmospheric carbon dioxide removal through direct ocean capture followed by durable storage. document_title: Isometric Air-Sea CO2 Uptake Module, Version 1.1
notes: The Isometric Air-Sea CO2 Uptake Module standardizes how additional atmospheric carbon uptake caused by a marine carbon dioxide removal intervention must be quantified. It applies to approaches that create a surface-ocean carbon-dioxide partial-pressure deficit, including coastal-outfall ocean alkalinity enhancement and direct ocean capture and storage. The module defines model-domain, physics, biogeochemistry, simulation, output, validation, uncertainty, documentation and crediting-timeline requirements and permits calculation through air-sea flux or dissolved-inorganic-carbon approaches with cross-checks. It relies on extensively validated ocean biogeochemical models because direct observations generally cannot isolate project-induced uptake across the necessary spatial and temporal scales. The module is a supporting accounting rule, not a deployment permit, standalone project approval or evidence that any removal has already occurred.

document_title: Isometric Dissolved Inorganic Carbon Storage in Oceans Module, Version 1.0

document_title: M0172 Methodology Framework for Seaweed Carbon Projects
notes: Verra's M0172 proposal is a globally applicable framework for seaweed carbon projects. The proposed structure would provide overarching rules used together with activity-specific modules, beginning with a module for creation of seaweed or kelp farms intended to increase carbon sequestration and storage in ocean sediments. The framework is designed to accommodate future modules for restoration and conservation of native seaweed beds and offshore cultivation. Verra lists the proposal at Step 3, Draft Methodology Development, under Sectoral Scope 17 for ocean carbon. It is not an approved VCS methodology and cannot currently be used as the sole basis for project registration or credit issuance. Key accounting, durability, ecological-risk and monitoring requirements remain under development.
source: Verra
status_note: Listed by Verra in 2026 at Step 3, Draft Methodology Development, under development ID M0172; no final methodology approval has been issued.

document_title: Puro Standard Microalgae Carbon Fixation and Sinking Methodology, Edition 2025
notes: This Puro Standard methodology establishes voluntary carbon-removal certification rules for Microalgae Carbon Fixation and Sinking. Eligible activities enhance local microalgae growth on engineered substrates containing bound nutrients and then sink the substrate and attached biomass rapidly into the deep ocean for storage exceeding two hundred years. The methodology specifies site eligibility, scale and deployment limits, environmental impact assessment, baseline data, ecological monitoring, quantification, modeling, uncertainty treatment, third-party verification and safeguards. Puro distinguishes the pathway from uncontrolled ocean fertilization because nutrients remain bound and export is deliberately controlled. Publication creates a crediting pathway but does not authorize marine deployment. Individual projects must secure applicable permits, demonstrate net removal and durability, pass independent audit and satisfy registry requirements before CO2 Removal Certificates can be issued.
source: Puro.earth

document_title: Puro Standard Marine Anoxic Carbon Storage Methodology, Edition 2025
notes: This Puro Standard methodology defines a voluntary certification pathway for Marine Anoxic Carbon Storage. The approach deposits sustainably sourced, lignin-rich terrestrial biomass in deep, oxygen-depleted marine basins where microbial decomposition and animal disturbance are strongly limited, supporting storage for more than two hundred years. The methodology includes site screening, biomass sourcing requirements, baseline and counterfactual assessment, lifecycle greenhouse-gas accounting, durability analysis, monitoring, modeling, field sampling, adaptive management and environmental and social safeguards. It is an active crediting standard but not a dumping permit or deployment authorization. Puro reported that projects remained at the field-trial stage and that no MACS credits had yet been issued; every project must obtain all applicable permits and complete independent audit before CORCs are eligible for issuance.
source: Puro.earth
status_note: Approved by the Puro.earth Advisory Board in April 2025 and active with a conservative durability category exceeding two hundred years.

document_title: Puro Standard Direct Air Capture and Ocean Storage Methodology, Edition 2025 Version 1.1
notes: This Puro Standard methodology provides voluntary certification rules for Direct Air Capture and Ocean Storage. The pathway uses a controlled electrochemical reactor to split seawater into acidic and alkaline streams, exposes the alkaline stream to ambient air so that it absorbs carbon dioxide, re-equilibrates the acidic stream with alkaline rocks and stores carbon as dissolved bicarbonate and solid carbonate. The methodology applies lifecycle accounting, measurement, uncertainty, additionality, durability exceeding one thousand years, environmental impact assessment, water-quality controls, community engagement and third-party verification. It is a private crediting standard rather than a government marine permit. Project-specific intake, discharge, mineral use and storage activities must comply with applicable law, and no credits can be issued without validated net removal, monitoring, independent verification and registry approval.
source: Puro.earth
status_note: Edition 2025 Version 1.1 is listed as an active Puro Standard methodology with a durability category exceeding one thousand years.

document_title: CCER-14-003-V01 — Methodology for Coastal Salt-Marsh Vegetation Restoration
notes: This official CCER methodology establishes eligibility, baseline, quantification, monitoring, validation and verification rules for artificial restoration of coastal salt-marsh vegetation on suitable unvegetated tidal flats or areas vacated after specified human uses. Project-area and emission-reduction ownership must be clear, planted areas must be at least 400 square metres and the crediting period must be between twenty and forty years. The methodology accounts for soil organic carbon and, where woody vegetation is used, biomass carbon, while deducting methane, nitrous-oxide and non-permanence risks. It allows additionality to be deemed for qualifying public-interest restoration and requires geospatial boundaries, field or remote-sensing monitoring and auditable records. The methodology enables certification but does not replace land, sea-use or environmental approvals and does not itself issue CCER units.
source: Ministry of Ecology and Environment and Ministry of Natural Resources, People's Republic of China
status_note: Final Version 01 was released in December 2025 and is active for eligible projects in China's national voluntary emission-reduction market.

Eligible projects use a twenty- to forty-year crediting period and a baseline of continued absence of vegetation. The methodology quantifies changes in soil organic carbon, deducts methane and nitrous-oxide emissions and applies a non-permanence deduction, while allowing additionality to be deemed for qualifying public-interest restoration. Spatial boundaries and carbon strata must be tracked through high-resolution geospatial information and field monitoring. The document creates an accounting pathway but does not authorize planting, register a project or independently issue CCER credits.

document_title: Fourth Basic Plan for Fisheries Resource Management (2026–2030)
notes: The statutory fisheries-resource plan applies from 2026 through 2030 and combines climate-responsive stock assessment, ecosystem-based habitat recovery and a staged sea-forest carbon market pathway. It was built through a systematic review of 8,974 papers and targeted searches of government and non-government sources, with the explicit aim of supporting potential greenhouse-gas inventory reporting and carbon accounting applicable to the United Kingdom. The inclusion of managed coastal realignment evidence is particularly relevant to evaluating restoration claims and identifying where default factors are too uncertain. The database is an evidence synthesis rather than an adopted inventory rule or project methodology. Variation in definitions, sites, measurement periods and methods must be considered before transferring values, and literature inclusion does not validate every result. The dataset does not set official emission factors, determine additionality or permanence, approve restoration, register projects or issue carbon credits.
source: UK Environment Agency / UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology / National Data Library
status_note: Formally published on 17 September 2025 and made available through the government data catalogue, with files refreshed in July 2026.

document_title: National Seagrass Layer (England) — 2025 Revision
notes: The National Seagrass Layer collates current and historical polygon records for Ruppia and Zostera habitats in English waters from Natural England, the Environment Agency, Defra bodies and licensed third-party surveys. The 2025 revision provides an agreed current-extent layer based on the best available evidence, plus all-years data, confidence information and survey metadata. It supports marine protected-area assessment, Water Framework evidence, restoration planning and the mapping of a habitat recognised for biodiversity and carbon storage. The publication contains important caveats: seagrass is shown only where surveys exist; absence may mean no survey; point records are excluded; survey methods and accuracy differ; and some historical polygons indicate presence rather than reliable extent. It is therefore an evidence layer, not a complete national carbon inventory or a legal designation. It does not estimate verified carbon stocks or removals, approve restoration, define crediting baselines, demonstrate additionality or permanence, or issue credits.
source: Natural England / Environment Agency / National Data Library
status_note: Originally published in 2022 and formally revised in August–October 2025; the dataset is maintained on an annual basis.

notes: This case study applies an early version of Australia's guide for measuring and accounting for the benefits of restoring coastal blue-carbon ecosystems to the previously restored Tomago Wetlands in the Hunter River. subnational_area: Australian coastline and Indigenous Sea Country
document_title: Blue Carbon in Australia: Understanding the Opportunity for Indigenous People
notes: This technical report examines where Australian blue-carbon and emerging nature-repair markets may create realistic opportunities for Indigenous people and where legal, methodological and commercial barriers remain. It distinguishes the presence of healthy mangroves, saltmarshes and seagrass from the narrower conditions required for a crediting project, including degradation or threat, an eligible activity, recognised rights, consent and a suitable method. The report reviews the existing ACCU Scheme tidal-restoration method, voluntary standards and developing biodiversity markets and maps Indigenous legal or consent rights along much of the coastline. It stresses that management responsibilities do not always equal rights recognised by a market and that strong rights often have limited overlap with the currently applicable blue-carbon method. The report supports Indigenous-led decision making, free prior and informed consent, capacity building and policy reform, but it does not grant project rights, provide legal advice for an individual claim or approve a methodology. Opportunity mapping does not prove financial viability, additionality, permanence or credit eligibility, and no quantified removal or credit issuance is certified by the report.
source: Australian Government National Environmental Science Program — Marine and Coastal Hub / Indigenous Carbon Industry Network
status_note: Technical report published in 2024 as an output of NESP Project 3.20.

subnational_area: German high seas jurisdiction, including the German exclusive economic zone, continental shelf and marine subsoil
document_title: Erstes Gesetz zur Änderung des Hohe-See-Einbringungsgesetzes
notes: The First Act Amending the High Seas Dumping Act was promulgated on 13 March 2026 as Federal Law Gazette 2026 I No. 70 and creates a substantially broader German legal framework for offshore carbon dioxide storage and marine geoengineering. The amendment adds carbon dioxide streams intended for permanent geological storage to the statutory exceptions from the general prohibition on introducing wastes or other substances into the high seas and provides that storage in the marine subsoil under German sovereignty, in the German exclusive economic zone and on the German continental shelf is governed by the authorization rules of the KSpTG rather than by a separate dumping permit under the High Seas Dumping Act. It also establishes a conditional legal route for exporting carbon dioxide streams to another state for offshore geological storage where the London Protocol Article 6 requirements are satisfied. At the same time, the amendment updates the statutory definition and regulation of marine geoengineering and replaces the annex with a list covering ocean fertilization, ocean alkalinization, biomass sinking, mineralization of carbon dioxide in basalt of the upper oceanic crust and technically assisted redistribution of seawater, including artificial upwelling. These listed marine-geoengineering activities are treated as exceptions only when carried out exclusively for scientific research and are subject to a precautionary environmental-protection regime, including requirements directed at marine protected areas, biodiversity, human health, water quality, waste prevention, scientific quality, independent review and the absence of economic motivation for research. The Act is therefore both enabling for offshore geological carbon dioxide storage and restrictive for experimental marine carbon-removal interventions. Crucially, promulgation did not make the amendment immediately operative: Article 2 provides that it enters into force only when at least one of the relevant London Protocol resolutions, LP.3(4) or LP.5(14), becomes effective for Germany, and the responsible federal ministry must announce that date in the Federal Law Gazette. As of the current database update, the official consolidated High Seas Dumping Act still reflects the pre-amendment text and the commencement date has not been announced. The Act therefore does not yet constitute an effective deployment authorization for the listed marine geoengineering techniques or a project-specific storage permit.
source: Federal Republic of Germany — German Bundestag / Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety
status_note: Promulgated on 13 March 2026 as BGBl. 2026 I No. 70; entry into force remains conditional on LP.3(4) or LP.5(14) becoming effective for Germany and a federal commencement notice.

document_title: Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter (London Convention)
notes: The 1972 London Convention establishes the foundational international regime for controlling deliberate dumping of wastes and other matter at sea. Röschel and Neumann classify the London Convention together with the London Protocol as the only international treaty framework that directly and explicitly governs ocean-based negative-emissions activities when those activities fall within the legal concept of dumping. The Convention requires Contracting Parties to prevent marine pollution caused by dumping, prohibits or tightly controls specified categories of material, and relies on national permitting systems for activities that fall within its scope. In the marine CDR context, the paper explains that the framework can become relevant where a technique involves deliberate placement of substances or material into the ocean; later LC/LP decisions expressly brought ocean fertilization within this governance system. The Convention itself does not name modern mCDR technologies, does not authorize ocean fertilization or ocean alkalinity enhancement, does not establish carbon-removal accounting, and does not create carbon credits. Its ONCE relevance is therefore regulatory and precautionary: it supplies binding anti-pollution obligations and a legal basis on which later marine-geoengineering decisions and assessment procedures were built.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention
status_note: London Convention adopted in 1972 and in force internationally since 30 August 1975.
