document_title: 1996 Protocol to the Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter (London Protocol)
notes: The 1996 London Protocol modernizes the international dumping regime by replacing the older list-based approach with a more precautionary system in which dumping is generally prohibited unless a material appears on the permitted reverse list and the activity satisfies assessment and permitting requirements. Röschel and Neumann identify the Protocol, together with the London Convention, as the core direct international legal framework for ocean-based negative-emissions technologies that involve the placement or disposal of matter at sea. The Protocol is especially important because later resolutions under it created dedicated rules for ocean fertilization and a 2013 amendment designed to regulate marine geoengineering through a positive list, environmental assessment and permit system. The original 1996 Protocol does not itself endorse marine CDR, quantify climate benefits, establish a carbon-credit methodology, or make every ocean intervention subject to its jurisdiction. Its relevance depends on whether a proposed activity falls within the Protocol's dumping or placement rules and on the additional decisions and amendments adopted by Parties. It therefore functions primarily as a binding environmental safeguard and permitting framework rather than as a deployment-support instrument.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Protocol
status_note: Adopted on 7 November 1996 and in force since 24 March 2006.

document_title: Scientific Synthesis of the Impacts of Ocean Fertilization on Marine Biodiversity (CBD Technical Series No. 45)
notes: CBD Technical Series No. 45 provides an official scientific synthesis of the potential effects of deliberate ocean fertilization on marine biodiversity and ecosystem processes. Prepared by the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity after the international policy response to proposed ocean-fertilization activities, it reviews the scientific rationale for nutrient addition, the expected stimulation of phytoplankton production, the uncertain fraction of carbon exported and retained at depth, possible changes in food webs and species composition, oxygen and nutrient effects, biogeochemical feedbacks, and the limitations of current knowledge. The Röschel and Neumann paper uses this CBD assessment as part of the evidence base for understanding ocean-fertilization impacts and the precautionary governance response. The report is evidence-building rather than authorization: it does not approve field deployment, establish a carbon-credit methodology, demonstrate durable net atmospheric CO2 removal, or supersede the London Convention/London Protocol assessment system. Its policy significance lies in informing biodiversity safeguards and the CBD COP decisions that restrict climate-related geoengineering in the absence of adequate scientific and governance foundations.
source: Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity
status_note: Published in 2009 as CBD Technical Series No. 45; official scientific assessment supporting subsequent CBD ocean-fertilization and geoengineering governance.

document_title: Making a Short-Term EU Purchasing Programme Work for Permanent CDR
notes: This Negative Emissions Platform (NEP) discussion paper proposes a near-term European Union purchasing programme for permanent carbon dioxide removal before any long-term integration of removals into the EU Emissions Trading System is settled. Its recommended design combines buyer aggregation through an EU Buyers' Club, results-based per-tonne public support paid after Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming (CRCF)-verified delivery, private and Member State co-purchasing, recurring procurement rounds, and a pathway to larger-scale support associated with the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. The paper recommends beginning with a EUR 1 billion pilot in 2026 and argues for a diversified portfolio of durable CDR pathways. Its proposed eligibility discussion expressly includes direct ocean capture among the methods that could participate once an applicable certification methodology and other eligibility conditions exist, making the paper directly relevant to marine CDR policy and finance. The EUR 1 billion figure, however, is an NEP policy recommendation rather than an adopted EU budget appropriation or a binding European Commission procurement commitment. The distinction is especially important because the official EU CRCF Buyers' Club has subsequently become a real voluntary market platform, but the Commission states that, as of April 2026, its approved permanent-removal methodologies cover DACCS, BioCCS and biochar carbon removal; marine pathways such as ocean alkalinity enhancement and direct ocean capture are not part of that initial approved-methodology set. This record therefore captures a substantive quasi-formal policy proposal that could shape future marine CDR demand, not an existing authorization or guaranteed public purchase of ocean removals.
source: Negative Emissions Platform (NEP)
status_note: Published discussion paper dated December 2025 and promoted by NEP in January 2026; the proposed EUR 1 billion 2026 pilot is a recommendation, not an adopted EU appropriation or procurement award.

It targeted fundamental processes, regulatory mechanisms and engineered approaches for strengthening carbon sequestration in China's coastal and marginal-sea ecosystems, with particular attention to particulate organic carbon burial, microbially mediated refractory dissolved organic carbon production, carbon-sink indicators and measurement protocols, and demonstrations of ocean carbon-sink enhancement. These outputs make PACECS a major national research-and-demonstration programme directly relevant to ONCE science and engineering. The project nevertheless remained an R&D programme: draft indicators and measurement protocols were research outputs rather than automatically binding national standards, and the programme did not itself create a carbon-credit registry, authorize commercial-scale marine geoengineering, or establish a national compliance methodology for monetizing its experimental carbon-sink results. Its strongest policy function was to build the scientific, technical and measurement foundation for subsequent planning, standards and potential carbon-market applications. Global ONCE's official Partner's Projects page additionally states that invisible microorganisms including phytoplankton, bacteria, archaea and protozoa constitute a major component of blue carbon, and explicitly frames PACECS as research on ways to increase the ocean carbon sink and on technical foundations for engineering ocean carbon sequestration.

document_title: 国家级人工上升流增汇示范工程（山东鳌山湾）
notes: This national-level artificial-upwelling carbon-sink enhancement demonstration was developed in Aoshan Bay, Shandong, by a Zhejiang University team under the National Key R&D subproject on coastal blue-carbon sink enhancement. Zhejiang University reports that work began in 2017 and that all sea trials were completed by March 2020, making it China's first completed artificial-upwelling sink-enhancement demonstration project. The approximately 500-mu demonstration area integrated a marine-energy in-situ power platform, a data and automated-control centre, an ocean-environment and carbon-sink monitoring system, artificial-upwelling equipment and a large-scale macroalgae cultivation system. The artificial upwelling was designed to transport nutrient-rich bottom water to the euphotic layer, stimulate phytoplankton and macroalgal production and thereby enhance biological carbon uptake; the macroalgae component was intended to combine enhanced primary production with harvest-based removal of biomass. The project is important as an actual field demonstration rather than a purely theoretical study, and it generated operational experience on engineering, environmental monitoring and integrated aquaculture. At the same time, the demonstration should not be interpreted as a general legal permission for large-scale artificial upwelling in Chinese waters, as proof of durable net atmospheric CO2 removal at commercial scale, or as an approved carbon-credit methodology. Its function was experimental validation under a national R&D programme, with environmental performance, permanence, full lifecycle emissions and ecological effects requiring further evaluation before broader deployment.
source: Zhejiang University Ocean College / Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Programme
status_note: Field demonstration initiated under a National Key R&D subproject in 2017; Zhejiang University reported completion of all sea-trial tasks by March 2020. It was an R&D demonstration, not a general deployment permit.

document_title: The Octopus Desk — A Financial Marketplace for a Regenerative and Sustainable Blue Economy
notes: The Octopus Desk is a blue-finance marketplace initiative developed by ORRAA with Investable Oceans as part of the wider Sea Change Impact Financing Facility. Its stated purpose is to connect project developers, donors, investors and advisers, reduce fragmentation in the sustainable ocean investment market and improve deal flow for projects in the Global South. ORRAA's 2024 project materials describe a 'high-tech, high-touch' platform intended to match investors with investable opportunities, provide market information on financial performance, impact and resilience, and support greater consistency in impact measurement, key performance indicators, monitoring and reporting. The same materials identify blue-carbon investments for climate mitigation, resilience, adaptation and biodiversity regeneration, together with sustainable seaweed aquaculture, as initial platform focus areas. The 2025 Ocean Panel working paper repeats those focus areas and notes an intention to facilitate investment into smaller ocean-economy enterprises, including transactions beginning around USD 50,000, while standardizing aspects of impact reporting. This makes the platform relevant to both coastal blue-carbon finance and macroalgae-related ocean investment. The Octopus Desk should nevertheless be classified as enabling market infrastructure rather than as a carbon registry or certification system. It does not itself verify tonnes of CO2, guarantee that listed projects receive capital, create a compliance carbon market or authorize marine activities. Any blue-carbon or seaweed project matched through the platform remains subject to its own accounting methodology, environmental and social safeguards, legal approvals and investor due diligence.

document_title: Negative Emissions Technologies and Reliable Sequestration: A Research Agenda
notes: This National Academies consensus study provides a U.S. research agenda for negative-emissions technologies and gives coastal blue carbon a dedicated assessment. It defines coastal blue carbon as land-use and management practices that increase carbon stored in living biomass and sediments in mangroves, tidal marshes, seagrass beds and other tidal or salt-water wetlands. The report treats restoration, creation, managed transgression and nature-based coastal adaptation as potential carbon-removal pathways, while distinguishing true atmospheric removal from storage of externally supplied carbon-rich material. It recommends a substantial national research initiative and specifies research needs for basic science, mapping, long-term field networks, project deployment, monitoring and verification, permanence, environmental constraints, social incentives and permitting. The synthesis includes illustrative annual research-budget estimates for coastal blue-carbon work, but these figures are committee recommendations rather than congressional appropriations or awarded grants. The report also discusses regulatory barriers and the need to accelerate appropriate permitting without weakening safeguards. It is an evidence-building research strategy: it does not itself authorize coastal projects, issue carbon credits, establish a mandatory accounting methodology, or prove that any particular restoration project produces additional and permanent net removals.
source: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM)
status_note: Consensus study published in 2019; the study is complete, while its research recommendations remain a reference rather than an appropriation or deployment authorization.

document_title: IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC)
notes: The IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate assesses climate-change responses involving marine and coastal systems and is directly relevant to the evidentiary basis for ocean negative-emission governance. Its assessment covers coastal blue-carbon ecosystems and discusses proposed open-ocean interventions including ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and ocean alkalinization. The report recognizes that protection and restoration of vegetated coastal ecosystems can contribute to mitigation and provide adaptation and ecosystem co-benefits, while emphasizing limits on the globally scalable mitigation contribution and the need for reliable accounting. For more interventionist marine carbon-removal approaches, it highlights scientific uncertainty, reversibility, ecological side effects, monitoring and attribution difficulties, governance constraints and social acceptability. The textbook specifically cites SROCC when discussing artificial upwelling as an emerging ocean-engineering approach. SROCC is an assessment report rather than a regulatory instrument: it neither permits marine geoengineering nor establishes a carbon-crediting programme. Its policy significance is evidence-building, risk assessment and synthesis for governments, and its treatment of the technologies should not be read as endorsement of deployment or as a quantified authorization of net carbon removal.
source: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
status_note: IPCC assessment finalized in 2019; the report remains an authoritative scientific reference but is not a deployment permit or operating carbon-credit standard.

Because the transaction concerned macroalgal aquaculture, the engineering pathway is fishery carbon sink through macroalgae and the directly associated carbon-pump mechanism is BCP.

document_title: Revised Seaweed Beds and Tidal Flats Vision (Second Edition)
notes: Japan's Fisheries Agency revised the national Seaweed Beds and Tidal Flats Vision to strengthen locally coordinated conservation, restoration and creation of these habitats in response to accelerating environmental change. The second edition explicitly recognizes the importance of the carbon-sink function of seaweed beds and tidal flats and connects habitat management with Japan's carbon-neutrality objectives. It stresses sustained monitoring, participation by fishers and other local actors, adaptive management, and the need to treat habitat recovery as a long-term process rather than a one-off construction project. The agency also identifies blue-carbon crediting as a possible incentive that can support local conservation activity, while the vision itself does not issue credits or prescribe a national crediting methodology. This distinction matters because ecological recovery, net carbon benefit and market eligibility require separate measurement and verification. The vision is particularly relevant to seagrass and other shallow coastal vegetated habitats, where protection of existing stores can be as important as creating new biomass. It is retained as a strategic planning record rather than merged with later Ministry of the Environment evaluation guidance, Satoumi programmes or private voluntary credit standards, each of which performs a different policy function.
source: Fisheries Agency of Japan
status_note: Second edition published 8 December 2023 and used as current national fisheries policy guidance.

document_title: Satoumi Creation Guidebook — Revised Edition
notes: The Ministry of the Environment's revised Satoumi Creation Guidebook provides practical guidance for conserving, restoring and creating coastal ecosystems through collaborative local management. The 2026 revision places current Satoumi practice in a setting of climate change, biodiversity loss and changing coastal use, and includes checklists and planning considerations intended to help communities move from diagnosis to implementation and adaptive management. Blue carbon is included as one of the ecosystem functions that can strengthen the climate value of healthy coastal habitats, particularly seaweed beds, seagrass beds and tidal flats. The guide promotes multiple benefits rather than a carbon-only intervention: biodiversity, fisheries productivity, water quality, recreation, cultural use and local participation remain integral to project design. It is therefore relevant to ecological sink enhancement but should not be treated as a carbon-accounting standard. The guidebook does not determine additionality, permanence, leakage, ownership of carbon units or eligibility under a voluntary market. Instead, it provides an implementation framework that can improve ecological quality and monitoring, creating a stronger evidence base for any later climate accounting. It is distinct from the 2025 Satoumi policy recommendations and from the multi-year foundation-support programme, which are separately recorded because they are different official instruments.
source: Ministry of the Environment, Japan
status_note: Revised guidebook published in March 2026.

Climate change, marine-ecosystem degradation and biodiversity loss are treated as linked pressures, making blue-carbon functions relevant within a broader nature-positive framework. It also provides the policy rationale later reflected in Satoumi funding and the 2026 revised guidebook. The entry is kept separate from those instruments because recommendations establish strategic direction, whereas the funding programme finances selected organizations and the guidebook supplies implementation guidance. notes: Fisheries and Oceans Canada's 2026–27 Departmental Plan explicitly connects federal marine science with the Blue Carbon Canada partnership. notes: Portugal's Despacho n.º 7083/2026 launches procedures for a coordinated national programme to map and monitor marine ecosystems through 2035. The order covers habitats including seagrass meadows, macroalgal forests, shellfish beds, maerl and other structurally important marine communities and requires long-term monitoring, interoperable data infrastructure and governance capable of supporting restoration and marine spatial decision-making. It links the programme to Portugal's nature-restoration and marine-protection commitments, including the 30-by-30 protected-area agenda, and to climate objectives under the Blue NDC by calling for evaluation of ecosystem services and carbon sequestration. It also anticipates modern digital infrastructure, including integration with ocean digital-twin capabilities, and assigns coordination roles across national marine institutions. The order does not create carbon credits or assume that every mapped habitat is a net atmospheric sink. Its value lies in building the spatial, ecological and temporal evidence needed to identify carbon-rich habitats, track change and target protection or restoration. A coordinated programme proposal is required by 30 September 2026, so implementation details remain to be finalized. document_title: Microbes Mediated and Coupled Comprehensive Negative Carbon Emissions in the ocean
notes: This 2022–2025 Special Project of Carbon Neutralization of the National Natural Science Foundation of China, led by Nianzhi Jiao and explicitly listed by Global ONCE as a Partner's Project, uses the marine microbial carbon pump (MCP) as its core theoretical foundation. document_title: Global ONCE Triple REAL Vision
notes: Global ONCE's Triple REAL vision was introduced at the Third UN Ocean Conference in 2025 and presented as the programme's core guiding governance vision at COP30. It is a non-binding programme governance framework rather than a treaty or deployment authorization.

document_title: Global ONCE Process-based Certification Mechanism for Ocean Negative Emissions
notes: At COP30 Global ONCE officially presented a proposed process-based certification mechanism for ocean negative emissions. The mechanism responds to the difficulty of directly measuring complex marine carbon-sink outcomes by proposing a whitelist of negative-emission activities and shifting the certification focus toward scientifically verifiable and continuously monitorable carbon-sink enhancement processes. The official account frames it as a pathway toward marine-carbon-sink marketization and global public-good governance. It remains a proposed non-binding mechanism and is not equivalent to an adopted compliance-market methodology or an issued carbon credit.

document_title: ASMASYS — Assessing Marine Carbon Removal: Synthesis, Scenarios and Governance
notes: ASMASYS is a project of the German CDRmare research mission dedicated specifically to marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR). Phase I (2021–2024) developed a unified, transdisciplinary assessment framework for marine CDR options. Phase II (2024–2027) expands and applies the framework to mCDR implementation scenarios in Germany, integrating ecological, technological, economic, social and governance dimensions. The project also addresses regulatory conditions and governance needs for mCDR. It is a funded assessment and governance programme, not a field deployment permit or carbon-credit issuance mechanism.
source: German CDRmare Research Mission / ASMASYS
status_note: CDRmare project; Phase I 2021–2024 and Phase II 2024–2027, with Phase II currently active.
